Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

scrutiny 1.0.0

CRAN release: 2026-11-10

scrutiny 1.0.0 is a major release with many bugfixes and new features, but also many breaking changes. If you have used GRIM, GRIMMER, or DEBIT before, you will need to adjust your code.

You can let error messages guide you – indeed, this will often be necessary. You may read up on individual items below, but the release notes are not intended to be read all at once.

Key changes

Most calls to grim_map() or grim() need three new arguments:

# scrutiny 0.6.1
grim_map(pigs1)
grim(x = "5.19", n = 28)

# scrutiny 1.0.0
grim_map(pigs1, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer")
grim(x = 5.19, n = 28, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer")
  • x and sd are no longer strings but numbers. Since numbers drop trailing zeros, digits_x states the number of decimal places. For GRIMMER and DEBIT functions, there is also digits_sd.
  • items_averaged replaces items, which defaulted to 1, so it silently tested means of multi-item scales as single items.
  • data_type states whether the data are whole numbers ("integer"), as the tests assume, or "continuous", where they don’t apply.

Each of these can also be a column of data. This allows for their values to differ by row. If one is missing, the error will tell you how to provide it.

You will also meet these changes:

  • percent = TRUE is now x_meaning = "percentage".
  • The probability column of grim_map() is now exp_incon, and audit() renamed some columns, such as incons_rate to emp_incon. I had changed the name of that grim_map() column before, but the new name will remain.
  • Under the default settings, GRIM’s results for testable value sets are unchanged. GRIMMER no longer flags any consistent value sets and catches some inconsistent ones it used to miss. DEBIT is now exact. All three tests use exact integer arithmetic, and several rounding procedures were corrected; see “Test results” below.
  • grim_plot() is now grim_plot_grid(), which returns its plot instead of printing it.
  • The rounding functions, such as reround(), moved to the roundwork package.
  • New: grim_explain(), grimmer_explain(), and debit_explain() use plain words to explain a result, and explain_print() does so for mapper output.

The tests, their three mapper tiers, and audit() constitute the stable core of this release. Every function newly added in 1.0.0 is experimental and may change in a minor or major release later on. The same applies to the developer tools, such as function_map().

Breaking changes

Numeric inputs

  • x and sd are now numeric in grim(), grimmer(), debit(), and their mappers; strings are no longer accepted. Since numbers drop trailing zeros, the new digits_x and digits_sd arguments are required. They take one value per row in the basic and sequence mappers and one per group in the total-n mappers, as in grim_map_total_n(df, digits_x = c(2, 1), items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"), and must be whole numbers from 0 to 15. Alternatively, you can add digits_x and digits_sd columns to your input data. The total-n mappers will apply them to both groups. (See “Function interfaces” below on items_averaged and data_type.)

  • digits_* arguments or columns, as well as the integer digits of x or sd, may not exceed about 15 significant digits. This is the precision of the double data type. Beyond that, GRIMMER and DEBIT get exact results for large means, SDs, and sample sizes. Apart from the limit on x with n that they share with GRIM, and one of 2^52 on n with x missing, GRIMMER only refuses an SD from about 5e5 to 1e6 on, or an SE from about 3e5 to 7e5 on, for n from 2 to 4, and value sets with more than a million candidate sums; see ?grimmer and ?debit.

  • Mappers return digits_x and digits_sd as integer columns. grim_plot_grid() (formerly grim_plot()) reads the number of decimal places from them instead of inferring it from x.

  • The n, items_averaged, and absolute columns of mapper output are integer columns if all their values are whole numbers within the integer range.

Test results

  • GRIMMER tests every sum that rounds to the reported mean. Earlier versions only took the one nearest to x * n, so tests 1 and 3 could fail for a consistent value set whenever several sums round to the mean, which can happen once n reaches 10^digits_x. In a grid of such value sets, a fifth of the inconsistencies that scrutiny 0.6.1 found for means with one decimal place were false positives, as were 3% of those for means with two decimal places. The warning about this was removed. Thanks to Nathanael Larigaldie and @takua624 (#80, #84).

  • GRIMMER computes candidate sums and sums of squares in exact integer arithmetic. Floating-point comparisons could lose a candidate on a rounding bound, so some consistent value sets were reported as inconsistent, also for multi-item scales. For example, grimmer(x = 0.03, sd = 0.18, digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", n = 200) was FALSE, although seven 1s and 193 0s have exactly these statistics. Thanks to Ian Hussey (#86) and Aurélien Allard.

  • GRIMMER rejects sums of squares below the minimum that whole numbers with the reconstructed sum can have. For example, grimmer(x = 3.6, sd = 0.2, digits_x = 1, digits_sd = 1, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", n = 11) was TRUE, but 11 whole numbers that sum to 40 cannot have an SD below 0.5.

  • For n < 5, GRIMMER also rejects sums of squares that are large enough but unattainable: grimmer(x = 1.0, sd = 2.0, digits_x = 1, digits_sd = 1, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", n = 2) was TRUE, but the values would be 1 ± √2. For n >= 5, the minimum and the parity test suffice, so grimmer() is TRUE if and only if a sample of whole numbers has the reported mean and SD, except under rounding = "even", which lets a tie round either way. The reason for both new rejections is "GRIMMER inconsistent (test 1)".

  • A rounding bound is exclusive whenever a value exactly on it would round away from the reported number. This already held for "up" and "down", and now also for "ceiling", "floor", "trunc", "anti_trunc", and the "*_from" methods. Under "even", both bounds stay inclusive, because whether base::round() sees a tie depends on the binary representation of the value.

  • symmetric now affects the results of grim() and grimmer(), not only the show_rec values. threshold no longer affects "up", "down", and "up_or_down", which always round from 5.

  • "down_from" and "up_from_or_down_from" read threshold as "up_from" does: rounding goes down if the part cut off is at most threshold tenths of a rounding step. It used to switch at 10 - threshold, so "up_from_or_down_from" could span up to 1.8 steps, and GRIM with threshold = 9 accepted every mean at n = 57. Results at the default threshold = 5 are unchanged.

  • "anti_trunc" no longer moves a value that already has the required number of decimal places: 8.42 rounded to two decimal places is 8.42, not 8.43, as with Excel’s ROUNDUP(). A mean of 0.00 is therefore consistent under "anti_trunc"; it used to be FALSE.

  • DEBIT is exact by default. The mean of n binary values is k / n for a whole number k, but DEBIT treated it as continuous and accepted some SDs that no binary sample of size n can have. formula gains "exact", the new default; "mean_n" is the old behavior. "0_n", "1_n", and "groups", which always failed, were removed. With show_rec = TRUE, debit_map() also returns sum_lower and sum_upper, the smallest and largest k whose mean would be reported as x.

  • GRIM, GRIMMER, and DEBIT return NA for every case that cannot be decided: an infinite value, an n or items_averaged that is not a positive whole number, or a missing value that could decide the case either way. A missing value that could not is no obstacle: grimmer() with a missing sd is FALSE if x fails GRIM, and with a missing x if no sum of whole numbers admits sd; debit() likewise. A missing digits_* value gives FALSE if the value set fails with the decimal places the values show, and TRUE if it passes with so many that only these values pass: grim(5.2, 5, NA, 1, "integer") is TRUE. A missing n gives TRUE if data that are all the same value fit, and FALSE if no data of any size fit: grimmer(3.2, 0.2, NA, 1, 1, 1, "integer") is FALSE, since whole numbers with a mean of about 3.2 have an SD of at least 0.36. A few cases are still NA; see vignette("technical-notes"). GRIMMER and DEBIT also need n >= 2, since a sample SD divides by n - 1, unless sd_meaning = "sd_pop". Such cases used to cause an error or return an arbitrary TRUE or FALSE. The renamed version of grim_probability(), grim_exp_incon() returns NA for them too.

  • grim_exp_incon(), grim_total(), and the exp_incon column of grim_map() take the rounding method into account via new rounding and threshold arguments. The old formula, (10^D - N * L) / 10^D, assumes that each reported value comes from a single range of unrounded values, one step wide. Under the default "up_or_down", a tie is accepted both ways, so the probability is lower: 0.4 instead of 0.6 for n = 40 and two decimal places.

Function interfaces

  • grim_probability() is now grim_exp_incon() (the old name is deprecated), and the probability column of grim_map() is now exp_incon, the expected rate of inconsistency. In every audit() method for mapper output, including audit_cols_minimal(), the first columns are now all_cases, incon_cases (formerly incons_cases), and emp_incon (formerly incons_rate), in this order. For grim_map() output, testable_cases follows all_cases, and exp_incon (formerly mean_grim_prob) and ratio (formerly incons_to_prob) come last. testable_rate was removed: it is testable_cases / all_cases.

  • items is now items_averaged and has no default (#94). It is the number of items averaged into each score; the old name was mistaken for the number of scale points, and the old default of 1 silently tested means of multi-item scales as single items. Give it wherever it applies, as in grim(), grimmer(), their mappers, and grim_exp_incon(); use items_averaged = 1 for single items and percentages. Mappers also accept an items_averaged column. grim_granularity() keeps its default of 1.

  • GRIM, GRIMMER, and DEBIT have a new data_type argument without a default, since the tests only apply to whole numbers (for DEBIT, the binary values 0 and 1). "integer" data are tested as before. "continuous" data can have any mean and SD (for DEBIT, within 0 to 1), so the result is TRUE unless no data can have the value set, as with a negative SD, the reason of grimmer_map() is "Continuous data", and exp_incon is 0. A data_type of NA gives the result for whole numbers if continuous data would get the same, and NA otherwise. Like items_averaged, data_type is vectorized and may be a column of data, and the mappers return it as a column. Give it in grim(), grimmer(), debit(), their mappers, grim_exp_incon(), and grim_total(), as in grim(x = 5.19, n = 28, digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer"). grim_plot_grid() and debit_plot() leave out continuous data with a warning.

  • GRIM’s percent argument is now x_meaning, which takes "mean" (the default) or "percentage", as in grim(x = 71, n = 43, digits_x = 0, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", x_meaning = "percentage"). Like sd_meaning in GRIMMER and DEBIT, it says what the reported value is rather than switching a conversion on or off. In grim(), its mappers, grim_exp_incon(), and grim_total(), giving percent is an error that points to x_meaning.

  • In every mapper, the dots come right after the key arguments, so the arguments after them must be named in full. The total-n mappers gain an n argument for the column of totals, as in grim_map_total_n(df, digits_x = c(2, 1), n = "total", items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer").

  • The settings of GRIM, GRIMMER, and DEBIT come in one order in every function: what the reported values mean (x_meaning, sd_meaning, and DEBIT’s formula), then rounding, threshold, and symmetric, then show_rec.

  • grim_map(), grimmer_map(), and debit_map() are made by function_map() and have an explicit argument for every argument of grim(), grimmer(), and debit(), such as formula in debit_map(). A digits_* column of data that disagrees with the argument is an error. merge_items, extra, and testables_only were removed: use dplyr::select() instead of extra and dplyr::filter(exp_incon > 0) instead of testables_only. grim_map(x_meaning = "percentage") keeps x as a percentage instead of converting it to a proportion with a message.

  • The sequence and total-n mappers, such as grim_map_seq(), have an explicit argument for every setting of their basic mapper, such as rounding or threshold, with the same default. These used to be passed through the dots, which must now be empty. Existing calls are unaffected.

  • debit_map()’s show_rec defaults to FALSE, as in grim_map(); debit_plot() reconstructs the values itself. debit_map() output no longer has a rounding column. grimmer_map() no longer has show_reason: the reason column is always returned. audit() on grimmer_map() output no longer has a fail_test2 column.

  • audit() on sequence or total-n mapper output returns the per-case summary of audit_seq() or audit_total_n(). It used to apply the basic mapper’s summary, which counted the dispersed rows as reported cases. audit_seq() and audit_total_n() are deprecated in favor of audit(), which returns the same summaries and also has .by. audit_cols_minimal() lost its name_test argument.

  • Mappers accept any data frame and return a tibble. Character row names, such as study labels, are kept as a rowname column, except by the sequence mappers, which drop all columns that play no role in the test; case joins them back.

  • grim(), grimmer(), and debit() lost show_rec and show_reason, which were only meant for the mappers. They are vectorized over x, sd, n, the digits_* arguments, items_averaged, and data_type; all other arguments must have length 1. Recycling follows the tidyverse rules, so grim(x = c(5.19, 5.18, 5.17), n = c(28, 32), digits_x = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer") is an error.

  • grim_map() and grimmer_map() no longer multiply items into n: n is the sample size as reported, and items_averaged is a column of its own. grim_plot_grid() places tiles at n * items_averaged.

  • grim_map(show_rec = TRUE) returns the same five columns for every rounding method: rec_sum, sum_lower, sum_upper, rec_x_upper, and rec_x_lower. The rec_x_*_rounded* columns are gone. sum_lower and sum_upper are the smallest and largest whole-number sums that would be reported as x, and consistency is TRUE exactly if sum_lower <= sum_upper, so the columns cannot contradict the result. With x_meaning = "percentage", rec_x_upper and rec_x_lower are percentages, like x.

  • The sd_binary_*() functions take sd_meaning, as in debit(), and return the population SD under "sd_pop" and the standard error under "se". sd_binary_mean_n() takes the mean as x instead of mean, as the tests do; mean still works, with a warning.

  • grim_plot_grid() takes the number of decimal places as digits_x, as every other function does, and the color of the raster as color_raster, like the color_* arguments of grim_plot_line(). The deprecated grim_plot() keeps its old signature, including digits and raster_color; color_cons, color_incons, tile_alpha, and raster_alpha have no effect anymore.

  • split_by_parens(), before_parens(), and inside_parens() take the pair of delimiters as delim instead of sep, which is the decimal mark in decimal_places(). split_by_parens()’s check_sep is now check_delim. The old names still work, with a warning.

  • S3 classes start with scrutiny_ instead of scr_, as in "scrutiny_grim_map" (#39).

  • function_map(), function_map_seq(), and function_map_total_n() take the function to map as .fn instead of .fun.

  • manage_helper_col() takes the argument as arg instead of var_arg, and add_col instead of affix; the old names still work, with a warning.

  • Mapper settings that other functions need later, such as rounding, are recorded in a "scrutiny" attribute instead of S3 classes, which are now used for dispatch only. The "scr_rounding_*", "scr_percent_true", "scr_map_seq_disp_nonlinear", "scr_seq_df", and "scr_seq_test" classes are gone.

  • In *_map_seq() output, case is the row number of the value set in the input data; it used to count only the inconsistent rows. n and items_averaged are separate columns, also in *_map_total_n() output, and n is dispersed in steps of 1.

  • In every function, rounding must be a string and symmetric a single TRUE or FALSE; a numeric or logical rounding was silently read as a position in the list of rounding methods.

  • decimal_places() and decimal_places_df() match sep literally, as restore_zeros() and restore_zeros_df() match sep_in, and the defaults are "." instead of "\\.".

  • grim_plot_grid() and debit_plot() return their plot instead of printing it. grim_plot_grid() has an aspect ratio of 1, which can be undone with ggplot2::theme(aspect.ratio = NULL). It also has a new split_by_digits argument that returns one plot per number of decimal places.

  • The background raster in grim_plot_grid() shows consistent cells in grey and inconsistent cells in white, the inverse of grim_plot()’s former default. I acknowledge that this might confuse long-time users at first, and that it departs from the color scheme of Brown and Heathers (2017, Fig. 1) that was the key inspiration for grim_plot_grid(). However, it matches the broader emerging ecosystem of forensic meta-science software that ties in with GRIM. In this related work, relatively few dark points signify possible value sets against a white background. See, e.g., Hussey (2026) on combining granularity and bounds methods.

  • debit_plot() lost line_size, show_outer_boxes, and the tile_* arguments. Instead, each rectangle is drawn over a point at the reported mean and SD, so that value sets with tiny rectangles stay visible. Its labels are placed the same way on every run.

  • duplicate_count_colpair() requires at least two columns, and its rate_y is the proportion of y values that occur in x, as documented.

New features

  • grim_explain(), grimmer_explain(), and debit_explain() lay out the test of a single case in plain words. They are built from the numbers that decide the test, so they always agree with grim(), grimmer(), and debit(). explain_map() adds these explanations to mapper output as an explanation column, using the settings of the mapper call, and explain_print() prints them. Each one names the rounding method it assumes, and its first line lists items_averaged and data_type.

  • grimmer(), debit(), and their mappers, explanations, and plots have a new sd_meaning argument: what a value reported as an SD really is. "sd_sample", the default, is a sample SD, which divides by n - 1. "sd_pop" is a population SD, which divides by n, as with NumPy’s np.std() or Excel’s STDEV.P. "sd_sample_or_pop" accepts a value set that is consistent under either; grimmer_map()’s reason column names the one that passed. "se" is a standard error reported as an SD. This test is weak: from about n = 30 on, nearly every value set whose mean passes GRIM is consistent under "se". Thanks to Ian Hussey (#95).

  • percentage_of(), percentage_of_map(), and percentage_of_map_seq() check whether a reported percentage matches a count out of a total. add_up_to() and add_up_to_map() check whether subgroup sizes sum to a total; add_up_to_map() selects any number of columns with tidyselect. percentage_of_map() and add_up_to_map() have audit() methods.

  • grim_plot_line(), grimmer_plot_line(), and debit_plot_line() visualize the test of a single value set. Among all means or SDs within a range that could be reported with the given number of decimal places, they draw a square for each value that is consistent with the reported sample size, leave the others out, and indicate the reported mean or SD value. Squares are labeled with their values if there is space. By default, zoom = "close" shows the reported value and the nearest attainable one; zoom = "medium" widens to the nearest attainable one on either side, and zoom = "wide" shows a whole unit, which is 0% to 100% for a percentage.

  • grim_plot_rates() plots each study’s rate of GRIM-inconsistent value sets against the rate that random means would show.

  • grim_values() returns all means of n integers that would be reported as x, with the whole-number sum behind each, and grim_closest() the achievable mean closest to x. Both return a tibble with a case column and an items_averaged column, as grimmer_values() and grimmer_closest() do (#62).

  • grim_grid() tests every combination of sample size and fractional part of a mean with GRIM. It is primarily meant for studying GRIM itself. Its inconsistent cells are the background raster of grim_plot_grid(). grim_plot_grid() now also draws a raster for the "up_from" family of rounding methods instead of throwing an error, and has a threshold argument, like rounding, for the raster that show_data = FALSE draws on its own. Otherwise, the raster follows the mapper call, and a rounding or threshold that disagrees with it is an error.

  • grimmer_values() returns every pair of a mean and an SD of n integers that would be reported as x and sd, with the sum and sum of squares behind each. debit_values() does the same for binary data. grimmer_closest() returns the pair whose SD is closest to sd, like grim_closest() for means, and debit_closest() does the same for binary data. This is related to #59 but doesn’t conclude the questions raised there. These functions and the *_plot_line() functions require data_type, and "continuous" is an error there, since they list or draw the values that whole numbers can have.

  • grim_binomial() tests whether the rate of GRIM-consistent value sets is above what random decimal digits would produce, and returns a Clopper-Pearson confidence interval. grim_binomial_power() computes the power of this test.

  • audit() has a .by argument for summaries by group, as in audit(out, .by = study). Output grouped by dplyr::group_by() now gets an error that explains the problem, instead of “no applicable method”. Methods in other packages need the dots: audit.my_class <- function(data, ...).

  • scrutiny_meta() returns the settings that a mapper recorded on its output, such as rounding and sd_meaning, so that a report can state the conditions of a result. Printed mapper output names the settings that differ from the defaults in its header, as in # GRIM: rounding = "up". Combining the output of two calls with different settings with dplyr::bind_rows() is an error, since the rows would be read under the first call’s settings, and so is combining it with the rows of a plain data frame; adding columns, as with dplyr::bind_cols() or tidyr::nest(), works. rbind() and joins such as dplyr::full_join() are not covered and keep the first output’s record; audit() on sequence and total-n output rejects the rows they add, and value sets that occur twice, as from binding an output to itself.

  • New rounding strings "ties_up", "ties_down", "ties_away", "ties_zero", and "ties_even". Each names a complete tie-breaking rule ("ties_away" is "up" with symmetric = TRUE), so combining one of these strings with symmetric is an error.

  • function_map() gains .args_by_row, .args_fixed, .cols_helper, .cols_derived, a working .col_names, and .reported_variadic for tests in which the data determine the number of key columns (#42). function_map_seq() gains .var_bounds, which sets the dispersion limits per variable, so that a mean can go below zero while n stays at least 1.

  • Last but not least, the package gained a hex logo. It is a reference to the topos of flying pigs in Brown and Heathers (2017), which the authors continued as a running joke in their later joint work. Like value sets that fail a consistency test, assertions about flying pigs may raise concerns about trustworthiness.

Bug fixes

Consistency tests

  • A count such as a sample size, item count, or decimal count within floating-point noise of a whole number, such as 100 * 0.29, is used as that whole number, as the checks already took it to be. It used to be tested as is, which could flip a result, make a case untestable, or make disperse_total() and the total-n mappers treat an even total as odd: 40 - 1e-9 was split into 19.5 and 20.5 instead of 20 and 20. This applies to the tests and their mappers, grim_exp_incon(), grim_total(), the sd_binary_*() functions, disperse(), disperse2(), and disperse_total(), including their dispersion steps, and the steps of seq_disperse() and the sequence mappers.

  • debit() no longer reports consistent binary data with a mean of exactly 0.50 as inconsistent, and returns a result for means of exactly 0 and 1, which used to be NA. Under formula = "mean_n", a bound of the mean’s range that the rounding method excludes no longer counts as attained: debit(0.05, 0.20, 25, 2, 2, "integer", formula = "mean_n", rounding = "ceiling") is FALSE, since every mean above 0.04 has an SD above 0.20.

  • Under rounding = "up" or "down", GRIMMER’s SD check and parity check now apply to the same candidate sum of squares, so grimmer(x = 0.11, sd = 0.87, digits_x = 2, digits_sd = 2, items_averaged = 1, data_type = "integer", n = 64, rounding = "up") is FALSE. Thanks to Ian Hussey (#85).

  • grimmer() gives the reason "Negative SD" for a negative sd. It throws an error if it would have to test more than a million candidate sums, which takes an n of more than a million. Means of 1e7 and more used to get wrong results, since the sums of squares passed 2^53, beyond which a double no longer holds every whole number.

  • audit() no longer counts a case without a test result as inconsistent, and computes exp_incon, ratio, mean_x, and mean_sd over the cases with a result instead of returning NA if one has none. A rate or mean over no cases is NA, not NaN.

Sequence and total-n mappers

  • An error in a row of data names that row instead of coming wrapped in purrr’s “In index” context. In the total-n mappers, the row is that of the reported values, not of a hypothetical scenario.

  • reverse_map_seq() and audit() on sequence output reconstruct the reported values from the diff_var column. They used to infer them from the gap in the sequence, which failed when out_min or out_max cut it short, so that audit() could report the opposite result. Both now accept any dispersion, not only a linearly increasing one.

  • reverse_map_seq() finds the tested columns by name. After rename(), it used to return a dispersed value as the reported one; a renamed or removed column is now an error.

  • audit() on sequence output reports the results that the mapper recorded instead of re-testing reconstructed data, which could drop percent (now x_meaning), threshold, or symmetric and flip the result. It works with a dispersion of length 1, with output that has no rows, and with cases whose sequence out_min or out_max emptied. A consistent reported value set included by include_reported = TRUE counts once in hits_total, not once per dispersed variable. A count or distance that depends on an NA result, on a variable whose reported value is missing and so was not dispersed, or on rows removed from the output, as by filter(), is NA rather than counting such value sets as misses. So does audit() on total-n output for rows removed from a direction. A case column turned into strings is read as case numbers again, so that the rows come out in the order 1, 2, …, 10 rather than 1, 10, 2.

  • *_map_seq() functions disperse means and SDs down to zero, and means below it; they used to stop one decimal unit above zero. With include_consistent = TRUE, they skip cases without a test result. If there is nothing to disperse, they return a tibble with no rows but the usual columns, not one without columns.

  • seq_disperse() rounds its values to the decimal level of by, so that long sequences don’t accumulate floating-point error (#83). It applies out_min and out_max to from as well, and no longer includes from twice when dispersion contains 0. out_max = "auto" is no maximum, like the default NULL, so that it works as in the sequence mappers.

  • *_map_total_n() functions use an items_averaged column, and reverse_map_total_n() reconstructs the correct total for any dispersion. Functions made by function_map_total_n() work when created in another package (#69). An even total split into two equal groups is tested once rather than twice, so audit() on total-n output no longer counts one split too many. It leaves undecidable splits out of scenarios_total, its hits are NA where an undecidable split might be one, and its hit_rate is NA for a case with no decidable split.

  • *_map_total_n() functions return the other columns of data, and warn about a total that leaves no pair of group sizes within n_min and n_max instead of failing. A helper argument such as items_averaged must be a single value there; a vector was paired with the wrong groups in the "back" direction. The constant values stay with their groups in the "back" direction, too. Input columns named like the result columns (n_change, both_consistent, case, dir, and constant if given) or the reported values (x, sd) are an error instead of being overwritten, and so is a constant named like a column of the output. Grouped input is tested like ungrouped input.

  • grimmer_map_seq() and debit_map_seq() no longer disperse n below 2, and grimmer_map_total_n() and debit_map_total_n() default to n_min = 2, since a group of 1 has no sample SD. Under sd_meaning = "sd_pop" or "sd_sample_or_pop", where it has one, both tiers go down to 1.

Decimal places

  • decimal_places() handles scientific notation, counts numeric values correctly when sep is not ".", and returns NA for NaN, infinite values, and the string "NA".

  • restore_zeros() handles scientific notation, no longer introduces floating-point noise at high widths, and returns NA instead of "NA". It rejects a negative width and reports values that exceed a per-value width. restore_zeros_df() and decimal_places_df() handle columns that contain only NA, and recognize columns whose decimal separator is sep_in or sep. restore_zeros_df() no longer warns about a column without decimal places, such as n, or a single row.

  • decimal_places() no longer depends on options(OutDec = ). With a decimal comma, it used to count no decimal places in any number, which also misled restore_zeros(), seq_disperse(), the sequence mappers, and duplicate_count().

Other

  • split_by_parens(), before_parens(), and inside_parens() split each string separately; a string with an unusual number of separators used to shift the values of all later rows. Custom separators are matched literally. split_by_parens() errors instead of overwriting a column, handles NA and input without rows or columns, only warns about unsplit columns if cols is given, but always about columns split under check_delim = FALSE, never about columns with no values, and keeps the column order with transform = TRUE.

  • row_to_colnames() keeps a one-column data frame a data frame, and rejects a header that repeats, such as “M, SD, M, SD”. It skips blank header cells and trims whitespace, so that a blank cell above “Study” no longer gives the name ” Study”.

  • duplicate_tally() no longer counts missing values as matches of every other value, runs in linear rather than quadratic time, and treats NaN as missing. audit() finds its tally columns by the names duplicate_tally() gave them; it took every second column, so a selection or reordering summarized the wrong ones. duplicate_count() is linear rather than quadratic for named input, uses a named vector’s names as locations, drops unused factor levels, and works on grouped tibbles. duplicate_count_colpair() compares values as strings. All duplicate_*() functions write numbers out in full, so 100000 is the same value as 100000L and "100000", not "1e+05". A list-column or a matrix column is an error. duplicate_count() and duplicate_tally() keep the column names of a matrix, and duplicate_count_colpair() takes one. Blank strings, "NA", and "NaN" are missing values there, as in the other string-reading functions, so the blank cells of a table read with read.csv() are not counted as duplicates.

  • is_seq_linear() returns FALSE for sequences such as c(1, 2, 1). The is_seq_*() functions fill gaps left by NA values using the step size implied by the known values, return NA for a vector with NAs only if the answer depends on the missing values (any one or two values are linear), and test strings and factors by their numeric values. Anything other than a numeric, character, or factor vector is an error, such as a list, a data frame, or a logical vector with values other than NA. tolerance = 0 no longer makes every comparison fail, and the tolerance is never finer than the rounding error of arithmetic on the values, so seq_disperse() output around values of 1e8 and more tests as linear and dispersed. A missing string counts as a missing number, as does the string "NA".

  • grim_plot_grid() plots negative means at the fractional part of their absolute value, plots percentages with the decimal places they were tested with, works with show_raster = FALSE, extends its x-axis to the data when n is not given, and warns about any rows it leaves out instead of suppressing all warnings. It only says “Also visualizing” GRIMMER inconsistencies if there are GRIM inconsistencies as well.

  • debit_plot() draws the DEBIT lines for the smallest and largest sample size and shades the band between them; it used to draw a single line from a recycled n column. Its x-axis is labeled as the mean, and data without rows is an error.

  • A key column name such as x = "mean" can be passed in a variable or through lapply() and purrr::map(). .name_key_result works in all three function factories. function_map_seq() works for a mapper with a single reported variable. is_map_df() and the related predicates recognize only scrutiny’s own classes; they used to accept any class ending in _map.

  • reverse_map_total_n() rejects mapper output with rows removed or reordered. disperse() rejects a missing n_max, and disperse2() applies n_min and n_max to the group sizes rather than to their midpoint, and disperses from two numbers that are not consecutive as given rather than from their mean, which made the group sizes fractional. seq_disperse() disperses a factor by its label. The sd_binary_*() functions return NA for n below 2 and for a fractional n or count, reject non-numeric input, and recycle their arguments by the tidyverse rules, as do grim_granularity() and grim_items().

  • grim() and grim_map() no longer fail when n and items_averaged are integers whose product exceeds the integer range.

  • Errors about an invalid rounding or symmetric name the function that the user called. Many errors from base R or from internal code were replaced by messages that name the argument at fault. A factor where a number is expected, as from read.csv(stringsAsFactors = TRUE), is an error that says how to convert it; it used to be read by its level codes, or gave NA with warnings. audit() and grim_plot_grid() name the columns they need if any were dropped.

  • restore_zeros_df(), decimal_places_df(), and split_by_parens() ignore grouping and return ungrouped data; grouped input used to fail or leave columns unchanged. is_numeric_like() is FALSE for dates and times, which restore_zeros_df() used to turn into NA, reads a number next to a non-breaking space, and takes the strings "NA" and "NaN" as missing values, so that the *_df() functions no longer skip a column that has them. A blank string, as read.csv() leaves in a character column, is missing too: restore_zeros_df() used to skip a column with a blank cell without a word. decimal_places() gives it NA decimal places, not 0, and restore_zeros() makes it NA without a warning. before_parens() returns NA for a blank part, as inside_parens() does, so that split_by_parens() splits a blank cell into two missing values. Both take a part "NA" or "NaN" as missing, and row_to_colnames() skips it like a blank cell.

  • decimal_places_df() and split_by_parens() take a matrix, as restore_zeros_df() does, and name the function for vectors when given one.

  • decimal_places_df() and restore_zeros_df() warn about a column that isn’t numeric-like if cols is given, not under the default, and always if it was processed under check_numeric_like = FALSE, but never about a column with no values.

  • A column named like an argument, such as sep or width, no longer replaces that argument in restore_zeros_df(), decimal_places_df(), and split_by_parens(). seq_disperse_df() finds a caller’s variable named x or diff_var. The is_seq_*() functions test integers as doubles, so that their differences don’t overflow.

  • A 64-bit integer (integer64) vector, as databases return for counts, is an error that points to as.numeric(). It used to be read as numbers near zero, so that every test returned NA.

  • The mappers test a numeric column with a class, such as one from tibble::num(), as plain numbers. The sequence mappers failed on such an x, and every mapper on such an n.

  • grim_map() is about 2.5 times as fast, and grimmer_map() about 80 times.

Lifecycle changes

  • The rounding functions moved to the roundwork package, which scrutiny now imports: reround(), unround(), reround_to_fraction(), reround_to_fraction_level(), rounding_bias(), anti_trunc(), and the round_*() functions. Call them from roundwork, as in roundwork::round_up(); see roundwork’s changelog for their changes. The vignettes Rounding options and Rounding in depth moved with them. Errors about rounding, threshold, and symmetric still name the scrutiny function that was called, and are now raised even if data has no rows.

Deprecated

  • grim_plot() is deprecated in favor of grim_plot_grid(), which tells it apart from grim_plot_line() and grim_plot_rates().

  • grim_items() is deprecated. It only computed 1 / (n * gran).

  • grim_probability() is deprecated in favor of grim_exp_incon().

  • audit_seq() and audit_total_n() are deprecated in favor of audit(), which returns the same summaries.

  • restore_zeros() and restore_zeros_df() are deprecated. They put trailing zeros back into numbers as strings, which the tests no longer take. Give the number of decimal places as digits_x or digits_sd instead, and format numbers for display with formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2).

  • decimal_places_df() is deprecated, since it replaces the values by their counts, while the tests need both. Use decimal_places() in dplyr::mutate() instead, as in mutate(digits_x = decimal_places(x)).

  • is_numeric_like() is deprecated, since scrutiny no longer takes numbers as strings, and so are is_seq_linear(), is_seq_ascending(), is_seq_descending(), and is_seq_dispersed(), which scrutiny no longer uses: the sequence mappers record how far each value was moved in diff_var. These functions may be removed in a future version.

Superseded

  • sd_binary_0_n() and sd_binary_1_n() are superseded by sd_binary_groups(): sd_binary_0_n(group_0, n) is sd_binary_groups(group_0, n - group_0).

  • absorb_key_args(), check_mapper_input_colnames(), and manage_helper_col() are superseded by function_map(), whose mappers do what these helpers do for a handwritten one, such as managing helper columns through .cols_helper.

Removed

  • Removed after their deprecation in 0.5.0: grim_map()’s show_prob, grim_ratio_upper(), and the 15 functions around is_subset_of().

  • Removed: grim_ratio() (use grim_exp_incon(), which takes the rounding method into account), manage_key_colnames() (use absorb_key_args()), unnest_consistency_cols(), write_doc_factory_map_conventions(), and the re-exports of rlang’s enquo(), enquos(), as_name(), as_label(), .data, and :=. check_audit_special() was removed, since audit() now reaches audit_seq() and audit_total_n() itself.

  • Removed in the sense of no longer exported: check_factory_dots(), check_args_disabled(), decimal_places_scalar(), write_doc_audit(), write_doc_audit_seq(), and write_doc_audit_total_n().

  • duplicate_detect(), superseded since 0.3.0, was removed in favor of duplicate_tally().

  • debit_plot() and grim_plot_grid() map consistency to one scale for colour and fill, so that ggplot2::scale_colour_manual() with aesthetics = c("colour", "fill") restyles them. Consistent and inconsistent value sets are a stronger blue and red than before, as in the new grim_plot_line() and grimmer_plot_line(). Values that are consistent but were not reported are grey, like the consistent cells of grim_plot_grid()’s raster. The arguments for fixed styles were removed: debit_plot()’s color_cons, color_incons, rect_alpha, line_*, and label_*, and grim_plot_grid()’s color_cons, color_incons, tile_alpha, and raster_alpha.

  • seq_disperse() and seq_disperse_df() return numbers, not strings, and lost their string_output argument. A string from still sets the step size by its decimal places, trailing zeros included.

  • seq_length() and seq_length<- were removed; their names clashed with seq_len(). So were seq_endpoint(), seq_distance(), seq_endpoint_df(), seq_distance_df(), and seq_test_ranking(), which made decimal strings for mappers that no longer take strings. Use seq(from, to, by = 10^-digits).

  • Removed after their deprecation in 0.3.1: seq_disperse()’s track_var_change and seq_disperse_df()’s .track_var_change. Also, restore_zeros_df() and split_by_parens() lost ..., which only caught argument names from before 0.2.4.

  • grim(), grim_map(), grimmer(), and grimmer_map() lost tolerance as both tests now compare whole numbers exactly. GRIMMER’s test 2 no longer rounds reconstructed SDs, since every sum of squares that passes test 1 passes it, so "GRIMMER inconsistent (test 2)" is no longer a possible reason.

  • function_map() lost .col_control and .col_filler, which never worked.

  • disperse(), disperse2(), disperse_total(), and the *_map_total_n() functions lost constant_index, and function_map_total_n() lost .constant_index. The constant columns always follow n_change; move them with dplyr::relocate().

  • scrutiny uses the base pipe |>, no longer exports the magrittr pipe %>%, and requires R >= 4.3.0.

  • scrutiny requires purrr >= 1.0.0 (#87), dplyr >= 1.1.0, ggplot2 >= 3.4.0, and cli >= 3.4.0. It no longer depends on corrr, and it suggests ggrepel instead of importing it. When using ggrepel, it needs a version >= 0.9.3.

Documentation

  • vignette("technical-notes") is new. It describes how the tests treat missing values, including the few cases that stay NA although every value would give the same result, and the rounding, exact arithmetic, and decimal places behind the results.

  • The GRIM and GRIMMER vignettes were each split in two. vignette("grim") and vignette("grimmer") cover the basics, including how to explain a result with explain_print(); vignette("grim-in-depth") and vignette("grimmer-in-depth") cover the values behind a result, the sequence and total-n mappers, and, for GRIM, the GRIM statistics.

  • vignette("consistency-tests-in-depth") was updated (#74), the GRIMMER documentation was improved (#66), and “Related software” has new entries.

  • vignette("consistency-tests-simple") was removed, since vignette("consistency-tests-in-depth") covers the same steps. vignette("devtools") was split up: the SDs of binary data are now in vignette("debit"), and decimal_places(), seq_disperse(), and disperse_total() in vignette("consistency-tests-in-depth").

scrutiny 0.6.1

CRAN release: 2025-12-02

This is a fix for compatibility with testthat 3.3.0. Also:

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a bug in grimmer_map_total_n(), debit_map_total_n(), and the underlying function_map_total_n() (#81). This could also have lead to incorrect results, but only in total-N mapper functions with two or more key arguments beyond n, so the bug never affected grim_map_total_n().

  • Added a warning whenever GRIMMER runs. I recently learned about a bug that can lead to false positives in test 3 of the current GRIMMER implementation; see #80. The bug will be fixed in the next version of scrutiny (and the warning will be removed).

Minor changes

  • Updated the “Related software” article to reflect recent additions to the forensic metascience toolkit. Now, it also attempts to roughly categorize tools by usage.

scrutiny 0.6.0

CRAN release: 2025-08-22

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a bug in the DEBIT functions that could sometimes have resulted in consistency being FALSE when it should have been TRUE (thanks to @nrposner, #75). However, this seems to be a rare issue, and DEBIT is not widely used in any case.

  • Fixed a bug that could theoretically lead grim(), grim_map(), grim_map_seq(), and grim_map_total_n() to throw a warning and possibly even return incorrect results (also @nrposner, #75). However, this is even less realistic than the previous bug.

  • Compatibility with ggplot2 4.0.0 was ensured (@teunbrand, #78).

  • restore_zeros() now checks width more strictly:

    • It no longer truncates decimal numbers if width is specified but some elements of x have more decimal places than that. For example, in earlier versions, restore_zeros(c(0.12, 0.123, 0.1234), width = 2) would have returned c("0.120", "0.123", "0.123"): it silently cut off the 4 from the last value. An error is now thrown in such cases.
    • Also, width is now checked to be either a single whole number or a vector of whole numbers with the same length as x.

  • restore_zeros_df() has the same fixes as above.

  • is_seq_dispersed() now works correctly if NA values are present.

Lifecycle updates

Currently none. However, the next major or minor version will introduce breaking changes, removals (as announced in scrutiny 0.5.0 below), and possibly more deprecations.

scrutiny 0.5.0

CRAN release: 2024-09-22

The package is now released under the MIT license.

Breaking changes

  • The ratio column in the output of grim_map() and grim_map_seq() was replaced by a probability column. This means:

    • Numerically, the only difference is that probability is zero whenever ratio was negative.

    • Conceptually, it is much easier to interpret: it is the probability that a reported mean or percentage of integer data that has a specific number of decimal places but is otherwise random is GRIM-inconsistent with the reported sample size.

      For example, probability is 0.6 for a mean of 1.23 and a sample size of 40. The same is true for any other mean with two decimal places. Thus, a randomly chosen mean with two decimal places, ostensibly derived from integer data, has a 0.6 probability of being GRIM-inconsistent with the reported sample size.

  • In the functions around grim_ratio(), the x argument must now be a string. This is consistent with grim_map(), unround(), etc.; and it prevents erroneous results that could previously occur by omitting trailing zeros.

  • The GRIMMER implementation was debugged, so that grimmer_map() etc. may now yield different results in a few cases. In particular, the items argument now works correctly, thanks to Aurélien Allard and Lukas Wallrich (#58).

  • is_seq_dispersed() now correctly returns FALSE if different numbers of missing values at the start and end of x mean that x cannot be dispersed around from.

New features

  • The probability column (see above) is created by a new function, grim_probability().

Lifecycle updates

Deprecated

  • As a consequence of the above, the show_prob argument of grim_map() is now deprecated and will be removed in a future version. It no longer has any effect.

  • grim_ratio_upper() is deprecated and will be removed in a future version. It no longer seems very interesting (and likely never was), especially now that the GRIM ratio in general has taken a backseat.

  • All 15 (!) functions around is_subset_of() are deprecated and will be removed in a future version. In truth, they were always poorly written and widely out of scope for scrutiny.

Removed

All of these had been deprecated since scrutiny 0.3.0:

  • audit_list() was removed.

  • The sep argument in restore_zeros() and restore_zeros_df() was removed.

  • The numeric_only argument in duplicate_count() and duplicate_detect() was removed.

  • The na.rm argument in duplicate_count_colpair() was removed.

scrutiny 0.4.0

CRAN release: 2024-02-23

This version brings major performance improvements. Furthermore:

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a bug in audit_seq(): If the dispersion argument in the preceding call to a function like grim_map_seq() was specified as something other than a linearly increasing sequence, the "diff_*" columns in the data frames returned by audit_seq() may have contained incorrect values.
  • Similarly, audit_seq() and reverse_map_seq() used to reconstruct the reported values incorrectly if the dispersion default was overridden as described above. At least for now, the issue is handled by throwing an error if these functions operate on data frames that are the result of specifying dispersion as something other than a linearly increasing sequence.
  • Fixed a bug that incorrectly threw an error in grim_map_seq(), other functions made by function_map_seq(), as well as seq_disperse() and seq_disperse_df() if an input value was so close to out_min or out_max that the output sequence would be shorter than implied by dispersion / .dispersion , and if track_var_change / .track_var_change (see below) was TRUE. Again, note that the bug only occurred if an error was thrown.

New features

  • A new vignette lists the options for specifying the rounding argument that many scrutiny functions have: vignette("rounding-options").
  • Another new vignette shows the minimal steps to implement a consistency test using scrutiny: vignette("consistency-tests-simple").
  • The output of grim_map_seq(), grimmer_map_seq(), debit_map_seq() and any other function made by function_map_seq() now has a diff_var column that tracks the difference between the dispersed variable (see the var column) and the reported value. Following the diff_* columns in the output of audit_seq(), this is the number of dispersion steps, not the actual numeric difference.
  • The same diff_* columns are now integer, not double.
  • function_map(), function_map_seq(), and function_map_total_n() have a new .name_key_result argument that controls the name of the key result column in the output of the factory-made function. This is "consistency" by default, but other names will fit better for other kinds of tests. (The results of these tests must still be logical values.)

Minor changes

  • In duplicate_count(), the count column in the output tibble was renamed to frequency. This makes for a more streamlined frequency table and removes an ambiguity with duplicate_count_colpair(), where the count output column means something different.
  • In seq_disperse() and seq_disperse_df(), the track_var_change / .track_var_change argument was renamed to track_diff_var / .track_diff_var. The arguments with the old names are still present for now but will be removed in a future version. Also, the unit of these values is now dispersion steps, for consistency with grim_map_seq() etc. as well as audit_seq().
  • grim_total(), grim_ratio(), and grim_ratio_upper() now require x to have length 1.
  • The docs now link to functions when opened in RStudio, not just on the website.
  • Accordingly, the output of write_doc_factory_map_conventions() now renders links. The function also has a new scrutiny_prefix argument for use in another package.
  • The “Infrastructure” article was renamed to “Developer tools”; vignette("devtools").
  • Some dependencies that used to be suggested are now imported.

scrutiny 0.3.0

CRAN release: 2023-08-08

Duplicate analysis overhaul

The duplicate_*() functions now present their output better and have overall been streamlined. Read more at vignette("duplicates").

  • A new function, duplicate_tally(), marks each observation with its overall frequency. It is similar to duplicate_detect() but more informative.

  • In duplicate_count():

    • All values are now treated like character strings, so all can be checked. The numeric_only argument is deprecated and should no longer be used.

    • The output tibble has two new columns, locations and locations_n. These hold the names of all input columns in which a value appears and the number of these columns. Details are controlled by the new locations_type argument.

    • New ignore argument for specifying one or more values that will not be checked for duplicates.

  • In duplicate_count_colpair():

    • New total_x and total_y columns in the output show how many non-missing values were checked for duplicates.

    • New ignore argument as in duplicate_count().

    • The na.rm argument is deprecated. It wasn’t very useful because missing values are never checked for duplicates.

  • duplicate_detect() is superseded. It is less informative than duplicate_count() and, in particular, duplicate_tally(). Still, it shares in the overhaul:

    • As in duplicate_count(), all values are now treated like character strings, so all can be checked. The numeric_only argument is deprecated and should no longer be used.
    • The duplicate status of missing values is now shown as NA.
    • New ignore argument as in duplicate_count().

Bugfixes

  • Fixed a numeric precision bug in round_up_from() and round_down_from() that occurred when rounding numbers greater than circa 2100 with a part to be truncated that was equal to 5 on that decimal level (thanks to @kaz462, #43). These functions are called within round_up() and round_down(), and indirectly by all consistency-testing functions.

  • Fixed a bug in audit_seq() that displayed one “hit” found by varying a given reported value if there were no such hits. The other columns were not affected.

  • Fixed a bug in function_map() that displayed the wrong calling function’s name in case of an error.

Minor improvements

  • Documentation for grim_map_seq() and all other functions made by function_map(), function_map_seq(), or function_map_total_n() now displays meaningful defaults. Printing the factory-made functions is more meaningful, as well. Internally, they now work with rlang::new_function(), which allows for flexible metaprogramming.

  • The experimental function audit_list() is deprecated. Just use audit() instead. audit_seq() and audit_total_n() are now documented separately from audit() and audit_list().

  • The lifecycle package is now imported and used in formal deprecations such as that of sep in the restore_*() functions. The janitor package is no longer suggested.

  • Adjusted to new CRAN requirements for packageVersion() usage.

  • Some performance improvements.

scrutiny 0.2.4

CRAN release: 2023-01-20

  • New decimal_places_df() function that takes a data frame and counts the decimal places in all numeric-like columns.
  • Four new predicate functions centered around is_map_df() test whether an object is the output of a scrutiny-style mapper function for consistency tests.
  • Newly exported is_numeric_like() function to test whether an object (e.g., a string vector) can be coerced to numeric.
  • New grim_ratio_upper() function gives an upper bound for grim_ratio().
  • Changes in split_by_parens():

    • The function now uses a cols argument instead of the dots (...). This follows tidyselect development guidelines. The default, cols = everything(), is to select all columns that contain the sep elements (by default, parentheses). Set the new check_sep argument to FALSE to select all columns regardless.

    • All other arguments were renamed: they no longer start on a dot. Furthermore, .col1 and .col2 have been renamed to end1 and end2.

    • A warning is now issued if one or more columns can’t be split (or is de-selected from splitting). This occurs if a column doesn’t contain the sep elements.

    • Internal changes for compatibility with dplyr 1.1.0.

  • In restore_zeros_df() as well, the dots (...) were replaced by a cols argument, and each other argument no longer has a prefix dot. This follows the changes in split_by_parens(), but note the default selection restrictions by the new check_numeric_like argument. The optional check_decimals argument goes even further.
  • Prevent false-positive warnings when printing ggplot objects (they had occurred since ggplot2 3.4.0).

scrutiny 0.2.3

CRAN release: 2022-12-11

Some new features and bugfixes:

  • New audit() methods for the output of audit_seq() and audit_total_n().

  • New duplicate_count_colpair() function that checks each combination of columns in a data frame for duplicates.

  • New restore_zeros_df() function to easily restore trailing zeros in all numeric-like columns in a data frame.

  • New seq_length() function to extend or shorten linear sequences.

  • Bugfixes in the is_seq_*() functions.

  • Argument evaluation is now forced in the function factories: function_map(), function_map_seq(), and function_map_total_n().

  • Some possible corner case issues in split_by_parens() are now prevented.

  • Internal changes for compatibility with purrr 1.0.0 and tidyselect 1.2.0.

scrutiny 0.2.2

CRAN release: 2022-08-22

This is a patch for CRAN compliance.

  • The package now requires R version >= 3.4.0 and rlang version >= 1.0.2.

  • Subtle changes to split_by_parens() that users generally won’t notice.

  • Minor shifts in the documentation (e.g., vignette("consistency-tests") now has instructions on exporting factory-made functions.).

scrutiny 0.2.1

This is a patch.

  • It reduces the scope of some examples for CRAN compliance.

  • Minor vignette changes.

scrutiny 0.2.0

This is a massive release, with many new features and improvements all over scrutiny. Most notably, the package now includes an entirely new system for implementing consistency tests.

  • A new vignette lays out how to implement consistency tests using scrutiny’s infrastructure. It describes many of the features mentioned below.
  • GRIMMER support was added, as explained in another new vignette. All GRIM and DEBIT functions mentioned below have GRIMMER analogues. For example, grimmer_map_seq() is analogous to grim_map_seq().
  • Because of the new, stricter rules for consistency tests, the output of grim_map() no longer includes an items column by default. Instead, the numbers of items (1 by default) are factored into the output’s n column. This focuses the presentation on the essence of GRIM.
  • GRIM and DEBIT functions are now somewhat less likely to flag value sets as inconsistent. That is because measures were taken to reduce spurious, computer-induced differences when comparing floating-point numbers. The same applies to the new GRIMMER functions.
  • function_map() enables users to quickly create consistency test functions for data frames much like grim_map() or debit_map().
  • grim_map_seq() checks if GRIM inconsistencies might be due to small errors, and the true values might be close to the reported ones. It varies the inputs up and down in a specified range, holding the respective other ones constant, and tests all those combinations. For summaries, call audit_seq() on the results.
  • debit_map_seq() does the same for DEBIT.
  • The above two are powered by function_map_seq(), which allows users to easily create functions just like these for any consistency test. All that’s needed is a data-frame-level consistency testing function like grim_map() or debit_map().
  • grim_map_total_n() applies GRIM in cases where no group sizes are reported, only total sample sizes. It systematically matches possible group sizes (around half the total) with reported mean or proportion values, GRIM-tests them, and counts the scenarios in which both matches are consistent. For summaries, call audit_total_n() on the results.
  • debit_map_total_n() does the same for DEBIT.
  • The above two are powered by function_map_total_n(), which allows users to easily create new functions like grim_map_total_n() or debit_map_total_n(), provided a data-frame-level consistency testing function like grim_map() or debit_map().
  • On a lower level still, disperse_total() takes a total sample size (comprised of the two unknown group sizes on interest) and calls the appropriate group-level function: disperse() for even totals, disperse2() for odd ones.
  • seq_disperse() and seq_disperse_df() extend scrutiny’s support for string decimal sequences with trailing zeros. They construct sequences centered around the input; a use case not directly covered by base::seq().
  • Predicate functions around is_seq_linear() test whether a vector represents a certain kind of numeric sequence.
  • In debit_map(), the x column is now to the left of the sd column if show_rec is FALSE, in accordance with the show_rec = TRUE default.
  • debit() is now vectorized.
  • The functions around is_subset_of() and is_superset_of() functions now have stricter variants grouped around is_proper_subset_of() and is_proper_superset_of().
  • split_by_parens() now accepts any pair of separators passed to .sep as a length-2 vector.

scrutiny 0.1.1

This is a patch, mainly fixing a bug that used to affect the presentation of input data in grim_map()’s results. It needs to be emphasized that this bug only affected a convenience feature, namely the presentation of certain input data in the output, not the GRIM test itself.

  • Previously, if percent was set to TRUE, the x values were converted to percentages. Because they need to be presented as strings, percentage conversion involves restoring the correct number of trailing zeros. The bug, then, was that all the x values appearing in the output (not in the internal computations!) were restored to the same “length” as the single longest one. This was now remedied, and x values are restored to their individually appropriate number of trailing zeros.

  • Another bugfix concerns versioning. Previously, the package had an incorrect version number. It was now corrected.

  • The last change was to remove an outdated and potentially misleading paragraph in the documentation of reround_to_fraction().

scrutiny 0.1.0

  • This version includes an overhaul of grim_plot():

    • It extends the function to cover cases of decimals values greater than 2, using a gradient instead of a raster.

    • It enables data-free calls to grim_plot() with the new show_data argument. Resulting plots only display the background raster. This mirrors Figure 1 in Brown and Heathers’ GRIM paper. (Although grim_plot() as a whole is modeled after this figure, the default addition of empirical summary data is specific to scrutiny.) Like Brown and Heathers, users may wish to create such raster-only plots in order to demonstrate some principled points. The key parameters decimals and rounding can be controlled directly to make up for the lack of information from data.

    • The function now checks if all input means or proportions (x) have the same number of decimal places. If they don’t, it throws an error. This strict criterion can be circumvented by specifying the decimals argument. However, since each raster is specific to one number of decimal places (and hence cannot be interpreted regarding x values with a different number), the recommended solution is to plot x values separately — once for each number of decimal places.

    • The show_full_range argument was removed because I now think it is superfluous.

    • Previously, there was some space between the raster and the y-axis. It has now been removed.

    • Test result data points, shown in blue and/or red by default, are now built on top of the raster, which makes for a more distinct appearance.

  • Two new functions, reround_to_fraction(), and reround_to_fraction_level(), enable fractional rounding, inspired by janitor::round_to_fraction(). For example, they might round 0.4 to 0.5 for fractions of 2. What tells the new functions apart is that they come with all the flexibility of reround(). Furthermore, reround_to_fraction_level() is closer to a conventional rounding function than the other two.

  • The new version also fixes a bug in row_to_colnames(), rewriting the function’s core.

  • Another bug was fixed in grim() and grim_map(), concerning show_rec: For rounding strings that lead to four reconstructed numbers per x value rather than just two, it used to be the case that only the two values corresponding to the first of the two rounding procedures were displayed in the output tibble. Now, all four are displayed, bearing appropriate names.

  • Another bugfix is for the threshold argument in reround(), which didn’t work properly before. This used to affect higher-level functions such as grim(), grim_map(), debit(), and debit_map(), as well. The default for threshold is now 5 in all such functions. Note that rounding up and down from 5 has been fully functional independently of it.

  • Also in reround(), the rec argument has been renamed to x in accordance with general naming conventions. The decimals argument has been renamed to digits in accordance with naming conventions among rounding functions.

  • In split_by_parens(), ellipsis support was added to protect the user from silent, unexpected results following named arguments in tidy evaluation. The ellipsis package has been added to the Suggests field in DESCRIPTION.

  • In some high-level functions, internal checks now determine if the lengths of multiple arguments that are factored into the same internal function call are mutually congruent. That is, if two such arguments are length > 1, they need to have the same length (which will throw a warning). Otherwise, there will be an explicit and very specific error message.

  • Finally, some minor refactoring and other small changes that users generally won’t notice.

scrutiny 0.0.1

  • Added vignette about other packages for error detection, called Related software.
  • Exported grim_plot().
  • Minor refactoring.

scrutiny 0.0.0.9000

  • Added a NEWS.md file to track changes to the package.
